https://www.thevermilion.com/a-drone-exp.text: A drone exploded near the Trans-Balkan gas pipeline between Bulgaria and Romania A drone exploded in Bulgarian territory not far from the border with Romania and one of the most important energy infrastructures in south-eastern Europe. The episode occurred on 8 August 2026 in the Kardam area, … Written by: Jack Williams Published on: August 9, 2026 A drone exploded in Bulgarian territory not far from the border with Romania and one of the most important energy infrastructures in south-eastern Europe. The episode occurred on 8 August 2026 in the Kardam area, in north-eastern Bulgaria, near the Black Sea. There were no victims or damage to infrastructure, but the proximity to the Trans-Balkan gas pipeline makes the incident particularly delicate. Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev reported that the drone fell and exploded about one hundred meters inside the national territory, in a sunflower field, about a kilometer from the compressor station connected to the Trans-Balkan system. Bulgarian authorities are examining the remains of the aircraft. The Bulgarian Ministry of Defense later stated that evidence suggests that the drone was likely a Ukrainian “Maya” decoy drone and that it had not been intentionally directed at Bulgaria. Did the drone come from Romania? According to the reconstruction provided by the Bulgarian authorities, the drone came from the direction of Romania. The unidentified aircraft would not have appeared on the Romanian and Bulgarian radar systems nor would it have been detected by the NATO systems that monitor the area a stone’s throw from Negru Vodă, one of the points through which the gas networks of Romania and Bulgaria are connected. What is the Transbalkan pipeline As mentioned, the point is particularly delicate due to the Trans-Balkan gas pipeline, an infrastructure built to transport Soviet gas to the Balkans via Ukraine, Moldova, Romania, Bulgaria and finally Turkey with connections also to Greece and North Macedonia. In Romania one of the main routes crosses the country from Isaccea, near the Ukrainian border, to Negru Vodă. From here the pipelines cross the border into Bulgaria right in the Kardam area, where the drone explosion occurred. For decades this corridor was one of the main gateways through which Russian gas reached Türkiye and the Balkans. However, now that European energy balances have changed profoundly, also thanks to the construction of TurkStream, which brings Russian gas directly from Russia to Turkey crossing the Black Sea, an important part of the old Transbalkan has lost its original function. The networks were therefore progressively adapted to allow the gas to also travel in the reverse direction, restoring strategic importance to the infrastructure after the Russian invasion of Ukraine and the progressive reduction of European dependence on Russian gas. In fact, supplies from various sources can travel northwards through the Balkan network: Azerbaijani gas, liquefied natural gas arriving at terminals in Greece, supplies sent through Turkey and, in the future, a growing quantity of gas extracted in the Black Sea. Why the Trans-Balkan is important for Ukraine Ukraine’s position in the European gas market has changed dramatically in recent years. For decades Kiev was above all the large transit country used by Russia to bring its gas to the European Union. With the reduction and then interruption of most of these flows, Ukraine has instead needed to strengthen the routes through which it can import gas from Europe. The Transbalkan offers one such alternative. In 2025, Ukraine also used the corridor to import gas from Azerbaijan for the first time, via a route that passes through Bulgaria and Romania before reaching Ukrainian territory. The explosion one kilometer from the gas station This is what makes the position in which the drone fell significant. Kardam is not just a small border town between Bulgaria and Romania. It is one of the focal points of the energy system that connects the networks of the two countries and, through them, the Black Sea and the Balkans with Moldova and Ukraine. According to information communicated by the Bulgarian government, the drone exploded about one kilometer from the Transbalkan compressor station. There is no damage to the structure and there are, at present, no elements that allow us to claim that the gas pipeline was the target of the aircraft. The geographical coincidence, however, remains relevant: the accident occurred next to an infrastructure which, created to bring Russian gas to Turkey, has become one of the possible alternative energy routes through which Ukraine can receive supplies from south-eastern Europe. https://www.theguardian.com/business/202.text: Record sales of EVs and hybrids bolstered spending in the quarter, the ABS said, accounting for three-quarters of the 0.4% quarterly growth in consumption. Photograph: Con Chronis/AAP View image in fullscreen Record sales of EVs and hybrids bolstered spending in the quarter, the ABS said, accounting for three-quarters of the 0.4% quarterly growth in consumption. Photograph: Con Chronis/AAP Australian economy We’re purchasing EVs instead of holidaying in Europe – and what else we learned from Australia’s national accounts ABS’s snapshot of Australia’s accounts shows economic growth – albeit low – in the face ‘challenging international circumstances’ Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Patrick Commins Economics editor Wed 2 Sep 2026 11.00 EDT Last modified on Wed 2 Sep 2026 11.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The Australian Bureau of Statistics released its latest set of national accounts, which give us a snapshot of how the economy is performing in the quarter, and what’s happening under the hood. Here are the three things you need to know. The economy is slowing, not collapsing Economic growth eased from 2.5% in the year to the March quarter, to 2.1% in the year to June, the Australian Bureau of Statistics figures showed, while real GDP in the three months to June expanded by 0.4%, a tick higher than in the previous quarter. Growth is softening, but is not disastrously slow, and there’s no sign of the collapse that many feared when the US and Israel began their attacks on Iran at the end of February, triggering a global oil shock. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email Jim Chalmers called it a “robust result in challenging international circumstances”. “The Australian economy has obvious strengths, but we can still see in these numbers our three primary challenges: inflation, productivity and global volatility, and we know that each of these puts pressure on people,” the treasurer told reporters. Bar and line graph (superimposed) showing economic growth since 2019 and slowing of growth since beginning of 2026 Economists predict the economy will continue to slow through 2026, moving towards 1.3-1.5% growth by the end of the year as the Reserve Bank’s interest rate hikes and the high cost of living drag on spending and activity. Stephen Smith, a partner at Deloitte Access Economics, said “today’s accounts show too little growth and too much inflation”. This winter we didn’t fly north, but we did splurge on EVs Just as the pandemic led to some big swings in behaviours and spending patterns, so has this year’s big shock – the Middle East conflict. The national accounts showed disposable household incomes, after inflation, lifted by a respectable 0.6% in the quarter. That slipped to just 0.3% after adjusting for population growth, but it was at least positive. Belinda Allen, CBA’s head of Australian economics, said this showed households were “largely insulated from the Middle East conflict over the quarter” and there was “only partial pass through of interest rate hikes to date”. What we didn’t do was fly north for the winter. War in the Middle East put the dampers on international travel, not least as high jet fuel costs pushed up the price of air fares. Grace Kim, ABS’s head of national accounts, said “the number of Australians travelling overseas for the northern hemisphere summer fell for the first time since the Covid-19 pandemic”. So what did we spend our money on? Instead of holidays under the northern sun, we splurged on fuel-efficient and electric vehicles. Record sales of EVs and hybrids bolstered spending in the quarter, the ABS said, accounting for three-quarters of the 0.4% quarterly growth in consumption. Vehicle purchases jumped by 10% in three months as we continued to shift away from gas guzzlers in an attempt to protect ourselves from pain at the pump, both today and in the future, and were helped along by government subsidies. House prices could fall 10%, analysts predict, as fourth interest rate hike looms Read more Still, Smith said that absent the spending on fuel-efficient and electric cars, consumption was “far too weak to suggest households are shrugging off cost-of-living challenges”. That said, the household saving rate lifted from 6.4% to 6.5% – pretty much its 20-year average – suggesting households continue to add to their buffers. A bigger population is driving higher growth, not productivity While the economy is expanding, this is entirely due to a higher population – an unfortunate hallmark of Australia’s since the end of the pandemic. Growth in real GDP per person shrank by 0.1% in the three months to June (recalling overall total GDP expanded by 0.5%), and was zero in the previous quarter. Per capita GDP was up by only 0.7% over the year, still below its 2022 peak – and at this rate, won’t get there any time soon. It’s the broadest measure of living standards, and reflects the lived experience of many Australians labouring through a high-cost and low-growth economy. Jonathan Kearns, the chief economist at Challenger, said “growth in GDP per capita has clearly slowed compared with the pre-pandemic period”. Our lacklustre productivity performance explains stagnating living standards, and there was no joy in the national accounts by this measure. Real GDP per hour worked – the measure of labour productivity – was flat in the June quarter and 0.2% lower through the year. Kearns pointed out that it’s difficult to raise living standards when productivity growth has averaged just 0.1% since 2018. “Perhaps AI will eventually boost productivity growth and improve the trend in GDP per capita and living standards,” he said. “But that will take time and does not lessen the need for productivity-enhancing reforms and winding back red tape.” Explore more on these topics Australian economy Economics Australian politics Inflation Business (Australia news) news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Canberra ‘put on notice’ as AI-generated submissions bring false information into parliamentary inquiries ‘How do I not crumble’: from Australia, Akash and his brother wait for news of their parents in Nepal Australia’s economy limps along, but the RBA should take a closer look before raising interest rates again Joe is used to the uncertainty of running a small business. https://www.montanaoutdoor.com/2026/09/w.text: The Big Timber Is Talking: What Northwest Montana’s Wildlife Is Telling Hunters About 2026 Whitetails, Black Bears, Elk and More—FWP Region 1 Wildlife Manager Neil Anderson Shares the Outlook for Hunting Northwest Montana in 2026 Big timber, rugged mountains and a whitetail buck slipping through the trees. If that sounds like your kind of hunting, this week’s Montana Outdoor Podcast is for you. The Search for a Better Hunt continues as Downrigger Dale welcomes Montana Fish, Wildlife & Parks Region 1 Wildlife Manager Neil Anderson for a look at hunting opportunities in Montana’s northwest corner. From deer and elk to black bears, mountain grouse and waterfowl, Neil explains what hunters can expect—and what deserves some extra homework before heading out. Rigger once called this country home, so this conversation comes with a little extra enthusiasm. But there’s plenty here for anyone discovering Region 1 for the first time, too. Whitetails lead the way One of the most encouraging parts of the conversation is Neil’s outlook for white-tailed deer. Several mild winters and good recruitment have him optimistic! Hmm rumor has it hunters just might start seeing more mature bucks! Watch or listen for the details! Mule deer offer a different experience. Neil describes populations as steady to slightly increasing, with deer concentrated in pockets of suitable habitat. He gives some great suggestions on where to find them! Black bears and a patchy berry crop Region 1 is also known for its black bears, but this year’s food supply could affect where hunters find them. Neil describes the huckleberry crop as spotty, with other berry crops struggling in some places as well. Productive berry patches may concentrate bears, while wetter areas near streams and other water sources can become increasingly important. Neil tells you where you’ll find those areas…Odds increased? Check! The discussion also turns to grizzlies and the importance of preparing for bear encounters. Rigger and Neil cover accessible bear spray, expiration dates, food storage and handling harvested game. Review the FWP bear-safety resources with the link below. Encouraging elk trends—and details worth checking Neil reports encouraging elk calf recruitment in areas where surveys are possible. He also discusses research around Thompson Falls and Noxon indicating gradual population growth over time. Plus he’ll give you the hunting districts that should be the places to start! Bring your bird-hunting plans, too Neil’s gives a great report on mountain grouse from Ruffed, Spruce and Dusky grouse you will get some useful info to help you plan a great grouse hunt. Turkeys provide another opportunity, with Neil describing a growing population and places to look. The conversation also covers pheasants, Hungarian partridge, ducks and geese, including opportunities around Ninepipe, the north shore of Flathead Lake and more! Access, preparation and the people behind the wildlife Neil describes a region with substantial public land, extensive Block Management opportunities and conservation easements helping protect access for future generations. As well as solid info on how to prepare if Region 1 is new to you. There’s more in this episode, including mountain lions, wolves, moose, bighorn sheep and wildlife research. Neil also explains why hunters’ observations matter, particularly in heavily forested country where counting animals from the air can be difficult. And before the conversation ends, there’s an unexpected wildlife story: a coordinated effort to vaccinate hundreds of bats against white-nose syndrome. Oh and he tells a very funny story about some Canadian Monties that were about to site some hunters big time for wandering across the border and hunting in the wrong country, that is until the hunters told Monties that THEY were actually in the wrong country! Oh Canada!! Watch or listen to this week’s Montana Outdoor Podcast for the full Region 1 hunting preview. Come for the hunting information, stay for the stories, and get ready to explore one of Montana’s most beautiful corners. Our thanks to Rocky Mountain Truck and Trailer and Superior Hardwoods of Montana for supporting the Montana Outdoor Podcast. https://www.politico.eu/article/france-p.text: A fresh wave of demonstrations in France saw fewer early incidents on Saturday than the previous weekend, as tougher policing measures and local protest bans aimed at preventing violence and looting drew criticism from unions and left-wing leaders. French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said early Saturday afternoon that 135 people had been arrested across the country. “We counted 35,000 people in the public space; there were 60,000 on Oct. 17” at midday, he said at a press briefing. The protests come a week after numerous scenes of looting and clashes between police and protesters on the sidelines of peaceful marches over the cost of living and school conditions. Advertisement Advertisement The march in Paris remained peaceful by Saturday afternoon. Authorities changed the authorised route late on Friday to redirect protesters away from the capital’s city center in an attempt to protect businesses looted last weekend. Far-left presidential candidate Jean-Luc Mélenchon said the move was aimed at discouraging and sowing confusion among protesters. “Everything is made to trigger an explosion,” said Mélenchon as he marched with protesters in Paris. French President Emmanuel Macron “will realize that this is going to happen every week,” he added. “We are the country of democracy, the country of human rights, and today this government is trampling on them. And that is very serious,” said Ryad Rani, president of the Union Syndicale Lycéenne, a high school students’ union. In Lyon, France’s third-largest city where gatherings were banned in parts of the city, the police used tear gas to disperse protesters. Nuñez, the interior minister, told police forces to be “uncompromising” with potential rioters earlier on Saturday, ahead of a day of protests that is leaving the country on edge. “Today’s key words will be mobility, responsiveness and adaptability, so we can really act against high-risk groups… We must be absolutely uncompromising and hyper, hyper, hyper-responsive,” he said during a visit Saturday morning to the National Police Academy in Vincennes. Advertisement Advertisement Nuñez was heavily criticized for his handling of last Saturday’s protests, and has been accused of underestimating both the number of protesters and the potential for violent incidents. He announced on Friday that 70,000 police officers would be deployed, 10,000 more than last weekend. The government has since imposed local curfews and banned public demonstrations in several cities including Lyon and parts of Nice and Lille. Macron also instructed local authorities to ban protests on Saturday except those organized by unions. The move drew backlash from unions, left-wing parties and human rights groups such as Amnesty International, which called the bans “serious restrictions of the right to protest,” and warned against a “slide toward authoritarian practices.” Authorities said that more than 10,000 people took part in an authorized anti-far-right march in Orléans, the Loire Valley city where Marine Le Pen’s National Rally is holding a party conference over the weekend. A banned protest is also expected on Sunday, when the far-right leader is set to formally launch her presidential bid. “Power prefers to barricade itself behind armored vehicles rather than listen to the legitimate demands of citizens,” said Manon Aubry, an MEP from Mélenchon’s left-wing Unbowed party, in a post on social media. The party supported the school protests in the run-up to last weekend’s riots, but sought to distance itself from the violence. France was also rocked by a deadly drive-by shooting in Trappes on Friday, which prosecutors are investigating as a terrorist hate crime. A 12-year-old girl was among those injured, according to local authorities . Advertisement Advertisement “This is a turning point because it is the first time there has been a terrorist act planned to kill our fellow citizens, our children, because of their skin color or the religion attributed to them,” Macron said after visiting the scene on Friday evening. His remarks quickly sparked criticism from several leading political figures, who slammed his description of it as the “first” terrorist act motivated by a person’s skin color or religion. Cost-of-living demonstrations have swept parts of Europe in recent weeks, with similar grievances bringing people to the streets in Spain, Italy and Albania.
